items.title: Lawn colour varies only in brightness, is calibrated to the greenest 30 % of pixels and the greenest scene; no dry or tan yards
items.current: build.py:249-250 `g = (rgb[:, 1] - rgb[:, 0]) / ...; pure &= g >= np.percentile(g[pure], 70)` (target colour = greenest 30 % of pure lawn pixels). :259 `lum_var = np.clip((sums / np.maximum(counts, 1)) / max(ref, 1e-6), 0.75, 1.3)` is a scalar, and :269 `tuple(base_tint * level / np.asarray(spec.tint))` multiplies R, G and B by the same level, so patches differ in brightness only, never in hue. :208 `n_variants: int = 6`; :220 `T.patch_ids(..., 25.0, seed)` (25 m patches). Dry ground only appears if the region's median green fraction is below 0 (build.py:171-173: `dry = grassy & (green < 0.02)`), which never triggers in Iowa. sources/landcover.py:471 picks, among the clearest scenes, the highest median NDVI ('peak leaf-on'); :477 `years = (today.year,) if today.month >= 9 else (today.year - 1,)` (the flight sun date defaults to 15 July 2025, build.py:96). Lawn base texture and tint: materials.py:30 `Grass_Cut.mdl, 1.5, (1.20, 1.15, 0.52)`.
items.real_world: Unsourced (ISU Extension and Iowa State lawn pages were unreachable): in July, unirrigated cool-season turf in the Midwest goes tan/dormant in patches while irrigated yards stay green, so adjacent yards differ in hue, not just brightness. Sentinel-2 passes at about 10:30 local solar time (unsourced here), nearly the render's sun time, so the 10 m luminance already contains tree shadows, which RTX then darkens again.
items.proposed_change: (1) Use per-channel patch ratios: level_rgb = patch mean RGB / class target RGB, clipped to 0.6-1.5 per channel, so dry (yellower, redder) and lush patches differ in hue. (2) Calibrate lawn to the median (not the greenest 30 %) of pure lawn pixels, and report the percentile spread in the log. (3) Patch size 25 m -> 10-12 m (about one yard) and n_variants 6 -> 12-16. (4) Pick the Sentinel-2 scene closest to the flight date (or the median NDVI) instead of the maximum, and log scene date and year next to --when. (5) Soften double shadowing: compute patch luminance as a high percentile (for example 75th) within the patch instead of the mean. Acceptance: render a lawn-only crop and compare the CIELAB a* and b* standard deviation across 30 m blocks with the same statistic on the Sentinel-2 grid used for calibration, within 30 %.
items.risk: BUILD_VERSION bump (changes materials and terrain mesh). More ground materials (currently 6 per class) raise material count; the scene-selection change makes builds non-reproducible across years unless the chosen scene id is stored in world.json.

items.title: Detected crown radius is computed but never used; tree width is just height scale times a 0.9-1.12 squash
items.current: vegetation.py:89 `crown = np.minimum(np.maximum(nn / 2, 1.0), 1.0 + 0.3 * ht)` and :90 `return np.column_stack([x, y, ht, crown])`; a repository-wide grep finds no reader of column 3. tree_instances uses only `trees[:, 2]` (height): :173 `squash = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.12, len(trees))`, :184 `np.column_stack([s * squash[sel], s * squash[sel], s])`. The model's crown aspect ratio (width/height) is therefore fixed per species; measure_model_height (build.py:649) measures only height.
items.real_world: Unsourced: open-grown yard and street trees are broader relative to their height than forest-grown trees, so crown width is not a fixed fraction of height. Crown width controls how much ground, shade and sky shows between trees, which is the first thing visible from 40 m at 32 deg down. The CHM-derived crown (nn/2) already carries this information.
items.proposed_change: Extend measure_model_height to also store each species' crown diameter at scale 1 (x-y extent of mesh points above 0.3 of the height) in tree_heights.json. In tree_instances set sx = sy = clamp(2 * crown / model_crown_diameter, 0.6, 1.6) (blend 50/50 with the current height scale to avoid extremes), independent small jitter per axis, and keep z = height scale. Acceptance, no tuning by eye: render cruise_nadir_chase over woods and yards, threshold green pixels, and compare the canopy-cover fraction with the CHM fraction above 3 m that data.py:264 already logs ('% of the area under trees taller than 3 m'); proposed tolerance +-5 percentage points, plus visible bare-lawn gaps between yard trees.
items.risk: BUILD_VERSION bump. Wider crowns increase overlap and can intersect roofs (trees are only dropped by trunk position, drop_trees vegetation.py:93-109); check house roofs in takeoff views.

items.title: Tree and shrub leaves are plain OmniPBR with no transmission or subsurface: backlit canopy will look dark and flat
items.current: NVIDIA's leaf MDL wrappers (fetched: Red_Oak_leaves_Mat, HoneyLocust_leaf_Mat1) are OmniPBR with diffuse_texture, roughness and normal textures, `specular_level` 0.5, detail_bump_factor 0.3, emission off, and no translucency, subsurface or diffuse-transmission parameter. HoneyLocust has reflection_roughness_constant 0.7 and Red_Oak 1.0, but both set texture influence to 1, so the roughness PNGs rather than those constants are what render. No opacity parameter appears in the wrapper MDLs either, so leaf cut-outs must come from the USD itself (unverified). The repo does nothing to the prototype materials (build.py:468 references them as is). rtx_look.py:131 `"/rtx/translucency/enabled": True,  # the prop-blur discs are translucent (drone_look.py)`; quadcopter_pbr.py:539 `enable_translucency=True`. nucleus.py:45-50 lists Kit materials including OmniSurface and AperturePBR_Translucent.
items.real_world: Unsourced numbers (leaf optical-property sources unreachable here): green leaves transmit a noticeable share of incident light, so a canopy seen against or under the sun is brighter and yellower than a front-lit one, and the waxy cuticle adds sheen at grazing angles. NVIDIA docs pages (docs.omniverse.nvidia.com, docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com) did not resolve from this sandbox, so whether RTX Real-Time evaluates diffuse transmission on OmniSurface is not verified here and must be checked on the PC.
items.proposed_change: A/B/C on one prototype in a test stage, camera facing the sun and then away from it (at 10:30 solar time the sun is at the elevation in world.json; decide which of cruise_front/cruise_back faces it from sun.azimuth_compass_deg versus heading_deg): (A) as is; (B) leaf shader swapped to OmniSurface with thin-walled and subsurface or transmission weights and the original albedo texture; (C) AperturePBR_Translucent. Keep the opacity cut-out. Metric: backlit canopy mean luminance divided by front-lit canopy mean luminance for the same species, plus a visual check for solid cards (cut-out lost). Keep the variant only if backlit foliage is not darker than the front-lit one and render time rises by less than about 15 % (proposed).
items.risk: Swapping the shader can drop the alpha cut-out and turn leaf cards into solid rectangles; behaviour differs between Real-Time and path tracing (--pathtracing); may be slower with 50,000 instances. A stage-time override avoids a map rebuild; authored edits to world.usdc need a BUILD_VERSION bump.

result.notes:
No file was edited, no code or Isaac Sim was run, nothing was installed or pushed. Only Read/Grep/Glob and web fetches were used.

SOURCING LIMITS (important). The shared WebSearch budget was already used up when I tried to search, and in this sandbox every host except GitHub and NVIDIA's public S3 bucket (omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com) failed DNS (cityofames.org, iowadnr.gov, extension.iastate.edu, fs.usda.gov, research.fs.usda.gov, nrs.fs.usda.gov, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, arxiv.org, sciencedirect.com, en.wikipedia.org, docs.omniverse.nvidia.com, docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com). I did not route around that. So every real-world reference in the items (Ames/Iowa species mix, ash loss to emerald ash borer, lawn dormancy, mowing, leaf transmission, crop canopy closure, roadside ditches, Sentinel-2 overpass time) is marked 'unsourced'. The sourced facts are the NVIDIA asset facts (tree, shrub, debris, leaf-material and texture file lists and MDL parameter values) fetched from the S3 listing URLs above, and facts from this repo. The agents on the PC should fetch the City of Ames street-tree inventory, Iowa DNR urban-forest data and USFS FIA Iowa tables (item vegetation-species-mix-spatial-coherence) and ISU Extension pages (lawn, corn/soybean canopy) before locking any numbers; all 'acceptance' thresholds I wrote are proposals for the test harness, not measured real values.

DERIVED GEOMETRY used in several items (arithmetic from repo values, not from a source): README lens 87 x 69 deg, 2048 x 1536 px (f about 1117 px, 0.74 mrad per pixel), cruise 40 m AGL, front camera 32 deg down in cruise (README.md:139-140). Back camera axis about 8 deg down in cruise is my inference (20 deg mount pitch minus the 12 deg lean); confirm it from camera_info.json before relying on it. With these, 135 m is the range at which a 10 cm leaf shrinks below one pixel; ground beyond 600 m occupies front rows 70-169 (about 6 % of the frame height) and back rows 611-686 (about 5 %), while the 3D tree zone (up to 600 m) covers roughly 6 % to 75 % of the front frame height.

CHEAP CHECKS WITH NO RENDER (do these first on the PC): (1) the build log line `[world] trees: ... red_oak N, ...` and ~/.cache/drone_scene/world_data/tree_heights.json (are the NVIDIA model heights reasonable, and is one species dominating through the height kernel?); (2) the log lines `canopy height (v2, 1 m): ...% of the area under trees taller than 3 m` and the ground-class shares (do any crop, wetland or ditch pixels lie on the route?); (3) a one-off test stage per tree species to read the canopy colour (item 1).

FOUND BUT OUTSIDE MY DIMENSION: (a) data vintage: sources/canopy.py:229-231 documents the canopy-height imagery as 2016-2020 (Ames 2017-04 to 2018-08), so trees cut or added since, including ash removals, are not reflected; a Sentinel-2 NDVI cross-check at build time could drop trees where the summer scene shows bare ground (not turned into an item because it has little visual effect). (b) The Sentinel-2 scene year follows the date of the build (landcover.py:477) while the sun defaults to 15 July 2025 (build.py:96): the ground colour and the lighting come from different years. (c) Wind: trees are static; leaf motion between frames is absent (adding it for 50,000 instances is costly, so not listed). (d) `data.tree_points` (OpenStreetMap single trees) is defined (data.py:156) but unused. (e) Tree leaf size scales with tree height scale (s = height / model height, vegetation.py:179), so very stretched trees have oversized leaves; this is invisible at 5.6 cm per pixel but matters in takeoff views near the backyard maple. (f) The CHM is integer metres and trees below 3 m are not detected, so a cap on `--max-trees` (60000, README says about 50,000 are built) would drop the shortest trees first (build.py:578-579).

items.real_world: UNSOURCED. Every web host except raw.githubusercontent.com and NVIDIA's S3 bucket was proxy-blocked and the WebSearch budget was used up, so I could not fetch a reference. If that holds, 'dark' (0.165) and 'grey' (0.285) are 1.5-3x too bright, and the roof palette should be mostly dark. items.current: STOREY_M = 3.0 (buildings.py:26). With floors: 'eave = fp.floors * STOREY_M'; otherwise small 'eave = 2.7', commercial 'eave = 6.0 + 4.0 * r1', farm 'eave = 4.5 + 2.0 * r1', residential 'eave = STOREY_M * (1 if r1 < 0.45 else 2) + 0.3' (3.3 m or 6.3 m). With a mapped height: 'rise_guess = 0.0 if flat else min(3.5, 0.25 * math.sqrt(area))' and 'eave = max(2.2, fp.height - (fp.roof_height or rise_guess))' (buildings.py:81-82), but the ridge actually built is 'rise = half_w * math.tan(pitch)' (buildings.py:194) with pitch 22-34 deg from r2, so the built top differs from fp.height by up to about +/-1 m (more for wide gables). WORK_LOG.md:191: heights exist for about 60 % of Ames buildings, the rest are the random split above.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED numbers (check against lidar): US one-storey eaves are about 2.5-3.0 m and two-storey about 5.2-5.8 m, so 3.3 m and 6.3 m are 0.3-1.0 m high, and floors * 3.0 is inconsistent with the +0.3 branch. A per-footprint 90th-percentile height above the ground would give real heights for every building, not 60 %. Shadows and parallax of 6-9 m buildings seen from 40 m make +/-1.5 m height errors visible as inconsistent shadow lengths.

items.real_world: UNSOURCED. Farm and outbuilding steel in the Corn Belt is mostly painted (white, tan, red, green, blue, charcoal) or galvalume grey; painted steel behaves like a glossy dielectric rather than a bare metal, so its colour comes from the paint, not from mirrored sky. Grain bins are galvanised corrugated cylinders with conical roofs about 5-20 m tall and are among the tallest objects in farmland. Residential backyard sheds are mostly wood or vinyl with shingle roofs. A metallic 0.9 surface under a blue HDR sky and sun looks strongly view-dependent (sky blue or dark, sun glints), which the cameras will see as flicker between frames.

items.title: Crop rows: open June-style canopy with tan soil blotches instead of a closed mid-July canopy
items.current: textures.py:35-36 `crop_rows(out_dir, name='crop_rows', *, size_px=1024, rows=4, spacing_m=0.76, growth=0.85, seed=0 ...)`, called with defaults as `textures.crop_rows(tex_dir, seed=k)` (materials.py:97). `half_w = 0.5 * spacing_m * np.clip(growth, 0.05, 1.0)` (textures.py:53) = 0.323 m, so canopy covers 0.646 m of every 0.76 m row pitch (edge wobble `edge = half_w * (1.0 + 0.18 * wobble + 0.10 * leaves)` :57, extra holes `cover *= np.clip(0.75 + 0.5 * leaves, 0, 1) ** 0.3` :59) leaving >=11 cm bare-soil stripes. Soil albedo (linear) `[0.18, 0.13, 0.09]` (:65) vs leaf `[0.055, 0.13, 0.035]`..`[0.09, 0.17, 0.045]` (:67). The module docstring itself says growth 0.95 ~ July corn and 0.4 ~ June soybean (textures.py:5-6) but the default 0.85 is what ships. I viewed the cached /root/.cache/drone_scene/world_textures/crop_rows_albedo.png: tan blotches (about 10-15 % of the area, 10-20 cm wide) in a horizontal band every 256 px (= 0.76 m) on mid-green; it reads as a patchy lawn or early-season crop. After the Sentinel tint (build.py:252-253) the soil stays a brown-grey with roughly 2.5x the red of the leaf pixels (derived from the constants above), so the blotches survive calibration.

items.title: Crop texture repeats every 3.04 m with strong contrast: visible lattice from 40 m
items.current: Tile is 4 rows x 0.76 m = 3.04 m square (materials.py:32 `3.04`, textures.py:39 `tile_m = rows * spacing_m`), 1024 px so about 3 mm/px. All noise is periodic over the tile (periodic_noise, textures.py:17-27). Inside one field the UV is `u = (c*x + s*y)/tile + offset_u` with one angle and one offset per field id (build.py:274-279, terrain.py:195-202), so the whole field is the same 3.04 m tile repeated with no variation, and `cover`/`wobble`/`leaves` features (0.06-0.25 m) recur every 3.04 m along the row. Field-to-field phase differs, but nothing breaks the repeat inside a field (hundreds of metres). Ground sample distance from the drone (derived: IFOV about 0.9 mrad at image centre, from the README 87 deg x 69 deg over 2048 x 1536): front camera in cruise 4-7 cm across track at 44-76 m, so one tile is about 45-80 px.
items.real_world: Unsourced: real crop canopies have no exact periodicity; plant spacing jitters, gaps and lodged patches occur at random, and fields show gradual large-scale tone changes (soil, drainage, tramlines). Any exact translation symmetry is visible as a regular lattice once the repeat is a few dozen pixels.
items.proposed_change: (1) Break the along-row symmetry without breaking row alignment: shift u by a random whole-metre amount per ~10-15 m cell (a shift along the row cannot misalign rows), implemented by splitting crop faces into several materials/offsets or, simpler, by baking 3-4 texture variants (different seeds) and assigning them per 12-20 m cell. (2) Make the texture bigger and less regular: rows=8, tile 6.08 m at 2048 px. (3) Add a macro tone modulation (smooth 20-60 m variation) at material level via the existing patch brightness quantisation, with more than 6 levels (see ground-patch-quilt). Measure: autocorrelation of luminance along the row direction in a rendered frame; the 3.04 m peak should drop below noise level.
items.risk: More materials means more GeomSubsets; the terrain mesh is already partitioned per material (usdio.py:86-92), so keep the count moderate (<= ~400 total). Along-row shifts across material boundaries must be exact multiples of nothing in particular (any shift along u is safe) but a shift in v (across rows) would cut the rows. Needs BUILD_VERSION bump and the cache-name fix described in ground-crop-canopy-closed.

items.title: Sentinel-2 B04/B03/B02 narrow bands are used as camera R/G/B albedo: vegetation will be too dark and too blue-green
items.current: `S2_BANDS_RGB = ("B04", "B03", "B02")` (landcover.py:95) are read as the R, G, B of the ground reflectance. The code path is otherwise correct on gamma/gain: calibration uses the raw linear reflectance `r["refl"]` (data.py:213,221, no 2.5 display gain, no sRGB curve), `mean_albedo` linearises the sRGB albedo textures (materials.py:79-84), `want = target / mean_albedo` (build.py:252), and far_albedo.png is the linear reflectance re-encoded to sRGB (build.py:372-375). So there is no sRGB-vs-linear mix-up; the issue is spectral. The same unmodified numbers feed the far terrain texture (build.py:372) and the horizon ring colour (build.py:608).
items.real_world: Unsourced (from memory of the ESA band definitions and typical camera filters; verify with the Sentinel-2 spectral response file and the LUCID/IMX265 colour QE curve): B04 is centred near 665 nm, 30 nm wide, right at the chlorophyll absorption minimum; B03 about 560 nm, B02 about 490 nm. A Bayer red channel is broad and peaks around 600 nm, so it also integrates the yellow-orange shoulder where leaf reflectance is higher, and green vegetation therefore looks more olive/yellow-green in camera footage than in an S2 B04-B03-B02 composite. Sentinel-2 L2A reflectance is a near-nadir bidirectional value at a ~10:30 local overpass (from memory), which suits the render's 10:30 sun but only for nadir views.
items.proposed_change: Introduce one S2_TO_CAMERA 3x3 (applied to linear reflectance before the class median, before far_albedo and before the ring mean) and test a grid: R = w*B04 + (1-w)*B03 with w in {1.0, 0.75, 0.5}, B = B02, G = B03. Compare chromaticity (r/g and b/g) of crop and lawn pixels in the rendered, white-balanced frames against real colour-camera aerial imagery of the same fields (e.g. a public true-colour orthophoto; none could be fetched here) and pick the w that matches. Keep sensor_sim's white balance untouched.
items.risk: Pure heuristic without a measured spectrum; verify the chosen matrix does not shift sky/ground balance (the sensor_sim auto exposure meters the clipped raw signal). BUILD_VERSION bump required. Do not stack with a separate tint hack on the same classes.

items.title: Ground at grazing angles (back camera): texture filtering is untuned and Fresnel sheen may brighten dark vegetation

Probe: horizon_front; measure ground-to-sky luminance ratio in the 10 px above/below the horizon.

I viewed the cached Leaves_BaseColor.png: a bright yellow and cream autumn birch-leaf litter. `lc.WETLAND: Grass_Winter.mdl` (materials.py:37; name suggests dormant grass, texture not viewed). `lc.MEADOW` and `lc.SHRUB` use Grass_Countryside.mdl (materials.py:31,34): viewed next to Grass_Cut the two PNGs have the same blade layout and brightness structure, i.e. a short fine-bladed mown-grass photo. Forest ground is exposed where no tree instance stands: trees are capped at `--max-trees` 60000 keeping the tallest (build.py:578-579, default at :80) and dropped near buildings and roads.
items.real_world: Unsourced: a mid-July forest floor seen through crown gaps is shaded, dark brown-green, with green understory; yellow litter is an October look. Unmown roadside, CRP and pasture grass in July is taller and coarser, with seed heads and straw-coloured streaks, not mown turf.
items.proposed_change: Forest: darken and green-shift the Leaves tint so the mean linear albedo is a dark neutral brown (value to be chosen by probe, no sourced figure) or substitute a procedural dark litter plus green understory; test in a crown-gap close view (climb_front near trees). Meadow: add a procedural tall-grass texture (reuse the crop_rows machinery with larger directional blades, 0.3-0.5 m mottling, straw streaks) for MEADOW/SHRUB and optionally scatter a sparse, near-route-only instancing of the existing Grass_Short prototypes. Wetland: view Grass_Winter first; if it is straw-coloured, calibrate it harder or swap.
items.risk: Forest class area is small near Ames (unsourced), so confirm a probe frame actually contains exposed forest floor before spending effort; meadow instancing near the route adds triangles and instances. BUILD_VERSION bump required.

items.title: Water is a glass-flat mirror with a near-black body colour painted on the terrain mesh
items.current: `WATER = MaterialSpec("water", color=(0.015, 0.025, 0.03), roughness=0.04)` (materials.py:41): no normal map, no texture, roughness 0.04, `# dark, mirror-like still water`. Water is just the WATER ground class burned from WorldCover/Overture water polygons and creek lines buffered to their width (build.py:160-164) on the same terrain triangles, so the surface follows the lidar ground (a channel for creeks), has no wave normal, no shore transition and per-patch random brightness (`lum_var = 1.0 + 0.08 * rng.standard_normal`, build.py:260-261).
items.real_world: Unsourced: Iowa creeks and farm or retention ponds are typically turbid green-brown rather than black, and wind or current ripples roughen the surface so reflections are soft streaks, not perfect mirror images. The standard Fresnel equations for n = 1.33 (derived) give a reflectance of roughly 0.06 at 60 deg from the normal (about the front camera's centre ray at 58 deg) and 0.3-0.4 at 80 deg (about the back camera's centre ray at 82 deg), so the body colour matters for the front camera and the sky reflection dominates for the back camera.
items.proposed_change: Give water a procedural fine-ripple normal map (low amplitude, anisotropic along the flow for creeks), roughness 0.08-0.15 (starting range, unsourced), turbid body colour of a few percent reflectance with a green-brown cast, and a 1-3 m wet-soil band at the shore (darker soil). Probe: any pond or creek crossing in cruise_front and cruise_back; check the reflection of the 3D trees and the sky reads as a soft, rippled mirror.
items.risk: Water area along a given route is small and unknown until the map is built; check the manifest or log (class histogram) first. Reflections of instanced trees in RTX real-time mode may be noisy at roughness below about 0.1. BUILD_VERSION bump only if the water material changes in the USD.

items.title: LOD tile seams: no shared edge vertices, one-sided border normals, 2 m skirts
items.current: `Lod.steps = ((60.0, 1.0), (200.0, 2.0), (450.0, 4.0), (900.0, 8.0)), far = 16.0` (terrain.py:39-40), tiles of 250 m (build.py:304), cell chosen from the tile's nearest distance to the route (build.py:310). Neighbouring tiles of different cell size do not share border vertices (terrain.py:5-8 docstring); each tile gets a `skirt_m=2.0` skirt (terrain.py:108, 133-148) carrying the top edge's UV and normal; vertex normals come from `np.gradient` per tile (terrain.py:101-105, 122), which is one-sided at the tile border, so adjacent tiles compute different normals at the same location. UVs are world-space functions (terrain.py:195-202) and the material is per face, so there is no texture or colour seam, only geometric and shading ones. The far zone uses 31.25 m cells with 1 km tiles that share vertices (build.py:348-351).
items.real_world: Unsourced: a real ground surface has no seams; at 4-13 cm per pixel (front camera) a crack or step of a few cm is sub-pixel, and the Iowa terrain is gentle (slopes of a few degrees), so I expect these seams to be invisible except at DEM discontinuities (ditches, terraces, embankments) where coarse-tile linear interpolation can sit decimetres off the true surface. Low expected impact, listed because the audit scope names LOD seams.
items.proposed_change: Probe only first: render a flat-lit (or high sun-elevation) frame over a tile border where the cell size changes (60, 200 and 450 m from the route, snapped to the 250 m grid) next to a build with a uniform 1 m cell for the same 400 x 400 m area, and subtract the images; flag any line with a luminance difference above about 2 %. If seams show: compute normals from the height function (central differences with the true neighbour samples across the tile border), not from the tile's own array, and stitch the coarse-side border vertices to the fine-side heights (edge snapping).
items.risk: Normal recomputation touches terrain.py shared by roads/buildings/trees seating (`Surface` uses the vertex Z, which edge snapping would alter); keep the Surface in sync (terrain.py:205-248). BUILD_VERSION bump if geometry changes.

Static audit only; no project code was run and no file was edited. Please note three process facts. (1) WebSearch was refused (the 200-call budget for the turn was already used up) and every WebFetch failed with `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND` (hosts tried: earth-search.aws.element84.com, registry.opendata.aws, www.nass.usda.gov, en.wikipedia.org, extension.iastate.edu). I did not try any workaround, so no web source was obtained and every real-world number above is marked 'unsourced' or 'derived'; none should be adopted as a target until the PC agents source it. The `sources` field is empty for that reason. (2) Before re-reading the rules I ran one read-only Bash `ls`/`find` to see whether the texture cache existed on this cloud machine (nothing run, installed or written). After that I used only Read/Grep/Glob. (3) I viewed the cloud machine's cached PNGs under /root/.cache/drone_scene (NVIDIA Base textures Grass_Cut, Grass_Countryside, Asphalt, Dirt, Leaves, Concrete_Rough, Soil_Rocky, and the generated world_textures/crop_rows_albedo.png). The generated crop_rows file matches the current algorithm (rows every 256 px) but I cannot prove it is not stale, which is the cache hazard flagged in ground-crop-canopy-closed.

Geometry facts used (derived, no source): IFOV about 0.9 mrad at image centre (87 x 69 deg over 2048 x 1536 px). Front camera in cruise looks 32 deg down (README.md:139-141): bottom edge 66.5 deg down (44 m, about 4 cm/px), centre 75 m (about 7 x 13 cm), top edge 2.5 deg above the horizon, so ground fills about 96 % of the frame and sky only about 4 %. Back camera (20 deg tilt minus 12 deg nose-down lean, my reading of the README) looks about 8 deg down: centre ground range 287 m (about 26 cm x 1.9 m per pixel), ground about 62 % of the frame, sky about 38 %. Ground farther than 450 m is about 7 % of the frame height in both cameras; the 6-22 km horizon ring is only a few pixels thick. Hence near-field ground texture (crops, lawns, roads) dominates the image area and the grazing-angle behaviour dominates the back camera. Sun at 10:30 solar time on 15 July at 42 N: about 62 deg elevation, azimuth about 130 deg from north (standard solar geometry).

Cross-cutting practical points for the PC fleet: (a) any change to the map or ground materials needs a BUILD_VERSION bump (build.py:48) or --force, and generated textures need versioned names (the crop texture is not versioned, see ground-crop-canopy-closed); (b) the S2 calibration path is otherwise consistent on linear vs sRGB (no gain or gamma confusion in the code), so the colour risks are the offset/date check and the narrow-band-to-camera mismatch; (c) suggested order of testing: ground-crop-canopy-closed, ground-s2-offset-date-sanity (cheap, read-only), ground-grazing-filter-and-sheen (settings only), ground-crop-tile-repeat-3m, ground-gravel-roads-misclassified, then the larger structural items (crop type, crop height). Items not found worth reporting: asphalt/concrete albedo (cached textures look plausible), the Overture/WorldCover class mapping (reasonable), and UsdPreviewSurface tint as UsdUVTexture scale (scene.py:359) applied in linear space is consistent with mean_albedo's linearisation, though the exact scale-vs-sRGB-decode order in Isaac's translator is unverified and worth one flat-patch probe (a patch of known tint under the calibrated sun, compare linear radiance with albedo x irradiance / pi).

verdicts.correction: Lines are right (materials.py:58-62 and :129, textures.py:200-201, buildings.py:91), but the derived albedos are about 15 % too high. textures.py:200-201 gives base 0.30 x tone (0.88 +/- 0.12, mean 0.88) x shadow-line factor (8 % of the area at 0.55, mean 0.964) = mean linear about 0.254. With the tint applied after sRGB decode that gives: dark about 0.14 (sRGB about 104), brown about (0.216, 0.173, 0.132), grey about 0.242 (sRGB about 135). materials.mean_albedo() on the generated PNG gives exact values. Real-world reflectances are still UNSOURCED: I could not reach any reference (only raw.githubusercontent.com and NVIDIA's S3 bucket resolve here, and the web-search budget is gone). Lead only, from memory and NOT verified: ENERGY STAR roof-product criteria (https://www.energystar.gov/products/building_products/roof_products/key_product_criteria, not fetched) set a steep-slope initial solar-reflectance floor of about 0.25, so typical dark shingles sit well below it. Measure on linear HdrColor radiance relative to a known reference (the lawn, or the 18 % grey-card line in drone_scene.log), not on display sRGB, because auto exposure changes pixel values frame to frame. The same 'tint applied after sRGB decode' assumption drives the Sentinel ground calibration (build.py:252); materials.calibrate_tints (materials.py:135) has no callers. So one probe that confirms the assumption validates both. The probe view 'cruise_nadir_chase' is not defined anywhere in the repo (grep found no definition); the fleet tooling must define it. GSD figures: lucid.py:168-169 gives fx = 4 mm / 3.45 um = 1159 px, not about 1080, so at resolution_scale 1.0 the front camera at 40 m AGL and 32 deg down sees about 6.5 cm/px across track, 12.3 cm/px along track, and 3.45 cm/px at nadir. items.real_world: Koschmieder: visual range V = 3.912 / beta_ext (2 % contrast threshold), so beta = 3.912 / V. My arithmetic for V = 20 / 30 / 40 km: beta = 0.196 / 0.130 / 0.098 per km; transmittance T = exp(-beta d) at 1 km 0.82/0.88/0.91, 5 km 0.38/0.52/0.61, 10 km 0.14/0.27/0.38, 22 km 0.014/0.057/0.12. So tree lines at 5-10 km should lose 40-85 % of their contrast and the 22 km horizon band should be almost pure airlight. The 20-40 km Iowa summer visibility is from the task brief; I could not source it (EPA page blocked by the proxy), unsourced. A secondary hobby-project note says a normal clear day is 40-100 km (weak, disagrees with the brief). Blue extinction is higher than red; Angstrom exponent about 1.0-1.3 for continental aerosol is quoted only in a secondary hobby doc, treat as unsourced; with alpha 1.3 and 550 nm as reference the factors are about R 0.80, G 1.0, B 1.30, which gives the blue-grey distance colour. The airlight colour is the horizon sky colour. Game-engine precedent: Bevy's city example derives its haze extinction from a 12 km visibility with the same relation.
items.proposed_change: Option B (recommended, works in both real-time and path tracing, no map rebuild): add `--visibility_km` (default 30, 0 = off) and apply haze in sensor_sim.py on the linear HDR before optics(): in HdrReader (quadcopter_pbr.py:388) also attach the Replicator `distance_to_camera` annotator to the same render product; in LucidSensor.process() compute T_c = exp(-beta550 * (550/lambda_c)^alpha * d) with beta550 = 3.912/V_km per km, lambda = 610/550/465 nm, alpha = 1.3, and L' = L*T + L_air*(1-T); sky pixels (d = inf/NaN or beyond far plane) are left unchanged because the sky already shows the horizon haze. L_air = median HdrColor of the sky rows 0-3 deg above the horizon (measured per frame from the sky mask, smoothed over frames) so it needs no unit calibration. Option A (try first for A/B, 1 hour): RTX fog `/rtx/fog/enabled`, `/rtx/fog/fogDensity`, `/rtx/fog/color` as used in NVIDIA's skill script (settings.set("/rtx/fog/fogDensity", 0.003) for a 40 m warehouse); the units and whether Isaac Sim 5.1 registers these exact names and honours them in the path tracer are unverified (rtx_look.apply logs a WARNING for unregistered keys); the density needed here is about 1.3e-4 per m, far below the 0.003 example. Option C: bake distance-dependent mix-to-airlight into far_ground/horizon_ground albedo (needs a BUILD_VERSION bump in world/build.py). Probe at V = 15, 30, 60 km and off.
items.risk: Needs a second AOV per camera (GPU memory/time). distance_to_camera on sky pixels may be inf, NaN or the far-plane value: mask them or the sky turns to airlight. Double counts if the new sky (light-sky-hdr-wrong-sun-elevation) already has a hazy horizon: keep airlight = measured horizon sky. Too-strong haze flattens contrast and the AE then lifts it (check light-ae-metering-includes-sky). RTX fog (Option A) does not depend on direction to the sun, so no forward-scatter glow toward the sun. No BUILD_VERSION bump for Option B.

items.real_world: Clear-sky radiance patterns depend on the sun zenith angle: here 28 deg off zenith vs the HDR's 47 deg. Hosek-Wilkie (1-10 turbidity, ground albedo 0-1, sun elevation 0-90 deg; range from the paper, unsourced here) is the standard analytic fit; Blender ships a reference implementation. The Poly Haven 'Kloofendal' sets are from the Kloofendal reserve in South Africa (from memory, could not fetch polyhaven.com), a dry high-altitude site; a humid mid-July Iowa day has a higher turbidity, a whiter, brighter horizon band and a paler zenith (qualitative, unsourced). Isaac Lab (newer main) neutralises RTX exposure on each camera before reading HdrColor for its own ISP: schemas OmniRtxCameraAutoExposureAPI_1 + OmniRtxCameraExposureAPI_1 with exposure 0.0, exposure:fStop 1.0, exposure:iso 0.0, exposure:responsivity 1.0, exposure:time 1.0, omni:rtx:autoExposure:enabled False, and documents 'do not combine with separately authored RTX exposure or tonemapping settings'. Whether Kit 107 has these schemas is unverified.

Hand calculation from lucid.py:99 (C4 lens k1=-0.10 k2=0.02, fx = 4.0 mm / 3.45 um = 1159.4 px): the pinhole render is 2298 x 1724 (3.96 MP, overscan 1.12) for a 2048 x 1536 (3.15 MP) sensor. Chain per frame: DLAA (1 sample per px, temporal) -> bilinear warp -> sigma 0.5 px Gaussian -> Bayer -> Malvar-He-Cutler -> sRGB -> H.264. Nobody has looked at the result: the stacked softening may make the video softer than a 3.45 um global-shutter sensor, or DLAA ringing may make it crisper than the sensor.
items.real_world: No sourced real LUCID Triton footage or MTF numbers: thinklucid.com, docs.omniverse.nvidia.com and dji.com do not resolve from the cloud sandbox and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so every real-camera sharpness number is UNSOURCED. Sourced facts about this setup: Isaac Lab's own test asserts antialiasing_mode DLAA gives /rtx/post/aa/op == 4 ("dlss = 3, dlaa=4"), source/isaaclab/test/sim/test_simulation_render_config.py:93 and :209; Isaac Sim's example gives the enum "0: Disabled, 1: TAA, 2: FXAA, 3: DLSS, 4:RTXAA" and "Set DLSS to Quality mode (2) for best SDG results". Geometry facts (hand-calculated from repo constants): centre IFOV 3.45 um / 4 mm = 0.8625 mrad = 0.049 deg per pixel; a real sensor with no optical low-pass filter point-samples the lens image, so distant fine detail (tree crowns, crop rows, roof edges at 0.5-2 km) alias on the real camera too.
items.proposed_change: Probe cruise_front and cruise_mid at --resolution_scale 1 (not the run_probe.sh default 0.5) and compare, using metrics.py sharpness and spectral_slope plus the montage.py detail crop: (a) baseline; (b) --supersample 1.5 and 2 (render 3447x2586 / 4596x3448, pre-filter already in sensor_sim.py:224); (c) grid_sample mode="bicubic" at sensor_sim.py:229 (add a SensorSettings.resample field); (d) blur_px 0.35 / 0.5 / 0.7 via a SensorSettings.lens_blur_scale override; (e) antialiasing_mode "TAA" and "Off"+supersample 2 as a ground-truth-ish reference. Variants (c) and (d) are pure sensor_sim changes and can be tested without re-rendering once camera-tool-hdr-resense exists. Also log the effective /rtx/post/aa/op and /rtx/post/dlss/execMode (see camera-tool-determinism-settings).
items.risk: --supersample 2 renders 15.8 MP per onboard camera (about 4x the pixels): slower and more VRAM, may exceed the probe time budget. A softer or sharper video changes the sensor-noise look and the H.264 bitrate. No map rebuild (no BUILD_VERSION bump).

items.title: Temporal AA / DL denoiser ghosting and shimmer at 10 m/s, rendered every 8th physics step
items.current: rtx_look.py:122 "/rtx-transient/dldenoiser/enabled": True (ray reconstruction, required by upperLowerStrategy 4 at rtx_look.py:120); rtx_look.py:126 samplesPerPixel: 8; quadcopter_pbr.py:539 antialiasing_mode="DLAA"; quadcopter_pbr.py:653 every = max(1, int(round(1.0 / (args_cli.fps * sim_dt)))) = 8 with --fps default 25 (line 70); quadcopter_pbr.py:764 render_now = capture, so the renderer sees one frame per 8 physics steps and the drone has moved 0.4 m between consecutive rendered frames. --motion_blur is off by default (line 106). Hand calculation for the front camera in cruise (body leans atan(0.021*10^2/9.81) = 12.1 deg, flight.py:241,308, so the camera is 32.1 deg below the horizon): at the lower frame edge (66.6 deg below horizontal) the ground is 43.6 m away along the ray at 40 m AGL, perpendicular speed 9.17 m/s, 0.21 rad/s = 8.4 mrad per frame = about 10 px of image motion per frame. History reprojection of DLAA and of the denoiser therefore has to cope with roughly 10 px/frame at the bottom of the image.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED: no DLSS/DLAA ghosting measurements were reachable (the NVIDIA DLSS programming-guide PDF was fetched from github.com/NVIDIA/DLSS but is compressed binary, unreadable here). The Isaac Sim motion-blur example pairs real-time motion blur with FXAA (aa/op = 2), not DLAA, and Isaac Sim's own notes (rtx_look.py:198-201) say Replicator rt_subframes > 0 breaks motion vectors (IsaacSim #722, unverified here). A real global-shutter camera has no temporal reconstruction at all, so any trail behind thin features (branches against sky, lane markings, grass edge at the field boundary, the drone's own shadow) is a render artefact, not realism.
items.proposed_change: Needs camera-tool-probe-motion first (the current probe holds the pose, so motion vectors are zero and cannot show ghosting). Then at cruise_mid and cruise_early render 25-frame lead-ins and compare 3 consecutive frames side by side with their difference image for: (a) DLAA (baseline); (b) antialiasing_mode="TAA"; (c) "Off" + --supersample 2 (spatial AA only, no history); (d) dl denoiser off, which requires /rtx/domeLight/upperLowerStrategy back to 0 or 1 (rtx_look.py:119-122 says strategy 4 needs the DL denoiser); (e) sampledLighting samplesPerPixel 8 vs 16. Judge: trails behind thin high-contrast features, flicker of tree crowns and crop rows between frames, GI boiling in shadows.
items.risk: Depends on camera-tool-probe-motion. Disabling the DL denoiser changes the sun/sky shadow noise and the sky-light strategy, so judge A/B at fixed exposure. TAA vs DLAA enum names go through rep.settings.set_render_rtx_realtime (simulation_context.py:803) inside try/except pass (lines 799-805), so a failure is silent: read the setting back. No map rebuild.

items.title: Auto exposure, hard clip and plain sRGB curve: how the ground and sky come out
items.current: sensor_sim.py:56 ae_target: float = 0.22 (mean of the clipped linear raw signal); sensor_sim.py:57 ae_speed: float = 0.35 (35 % of the way in log exposure per frame, time constant about 2.3 frames = 0.09 s at 25 fps); sensor_sim.py:234-236 _meter = float((raw_lin * k).clamp(0.0, 1.0).mean()), a whole-frame mean with no ROI; sensor_sim.py:282 rgb = rgb.clamp(0.0, 1.0) then srgb_encode (:283-285), no highlight roll-off, no S-curve, no black level. quadcopter_pbr.py:161 camera pitch 20 deg on the straight route. Hand calculation: at cruise the body leans 12.1 deg nose-down (flight.py:241,308), so the front camera looks 32.1 deg below the horizon (sky is about 4 % of the frame) and the back camera 7.9 deg below it (sky about 39 % of the frame height), so one AE target is metering two very different scenes. Exposure for an average 18 % grey scene works out at about 256 us from the constants in sensor_sim.py:45-48,204-207 (hand calculation, assumes scene_lux 100000).
items.real_world: UNSOURCED for the real LUCID Triton: its auto-exposure target, damping, ROI, Gamma default and any tone/LUT features could not be read (thinklucid.com unreachable from this sandbox, WebSearch budget exhausted). The README's claim "Like the camera's ExposureAuto = Continuous" (README.md:60) is therefore unchecked. Consumer drone footage usually has a filmic S-curve and shoulder; this pipeline has none, which is faithful to a raw machine-vision camera but not to typical drone video. Which of the two the owner wants as the realism reference must be decided before tuning.
items.proposed_change: Read exposure_us, saturated and mean_luma/clip_hi from probe.json and metrics.json for ground, climb, cruise_front, cruise_back, descent. Then A/B (all sensor-side, so use camera-tool-hdr-resense, no re-render): ae_target 0.18 / 0.22 / 0.30; metering ROI excluding the top third (so the back camera's sky does not set the ground exposure); ae_speed 0.35 vs 0.1; an optional soft shoulder (filmic curve) before srgb_encode with a SensorSettings.tone field defaulting to "none". Acceptance numbers to check against: metrics.py docstring guides (mean_luma 0.10-0.25, clip_hi under about 2 %), which are themselves unsourced rules of thumb.
items.risk: Exposure drives the whole look; compare at the same time-of-day sun. A tone curve makes the camera less 'LUCID-like' and the reported exposure_us less physical. No map rebuild.

items.title: Add small rigid-mount attitude jitter to the flight (none exists)
items.current: flight.py:303 StraightFlight.heading returns self.yaw (constant, set at :274); flight.py:305-314 rotation() is a pure function of the smooth SmoothMove acceleration plus drag (z = a + g + drag |v_air| v_air, :308); flight.py:242 wind: tuple = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0); flight.py:241 drag: float = 0.021. The cameras are children of the body prim (quadcopter_pbr.py:613 prim_path=f"{body}/{name}_cam") and the pose is written kinematically every step (quadcopter_pbr.py:711-713), so the video is a mathematically smooth glide with a constant 12.1 deg lean, zero roll, zero yaw wobble, zero gust response.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED numbers (no attitude-RMS source could be fetched). Geometry that makes it matter: one pixel is 0.049 deg at the image centre (3.45 um / 4 mm), so 0.1 deg of attitude noise is about 2 px, 0.3 deg about 6 px, 0.5 deg about 10 px of frame-to-frame image shake, at the control-loop frequencies (roughly 1-10 Hz, sampled fine at 25 fps). A rigidly mounted, gimbal-less camera on a real multirotor shows this; the owner's own flight logs or a real clip (estimate rotation jitter from homography/optical flow) should set the amplitude. Motor-frequency vibration (above 100 Hz) is frozen by a global shutter at about 250 us exposure and aliases, so it need not be modelled.
items.proposed_change: Add optional StraightFlight fields jitter_deg (rms, default 0.0), jitter_band_hz (e.g. 1.0-8.0), jitter_seed. In rotation(t) multiply by a small-angle rotation built from deterministic band-limited noise (sum of a few sinusoids with seeded random phases, a pure function of t so position/velocity/probe stay reproducible), roll and pitch at jitter_deg and yaw at about half of it, faded to 0 in the 'ground' and 'landed' phases (phase_name, :295) and applied in camera_matrix/camera_local consumers automatically. Probe 0 / 0.15 / 0.4 deg with the camera-tool-probe-motion clip; judge by the optical-flow RMS between consecutive frames against a real clip if the owner supplies one, otherwise by eye on the horizon line in cruise_back.
items.risk: test_flight.py asserts smooth poses: new fields must default to 0 so existing tests pass. Jitter shifts the probe stills slightly unless seeded per time. Too much looks like a bad gimbal. No map rebuild. Only visible in video or multi-frame probes, not single stills.

items.title: LMF2 propellers and guards are not part of the 1 % self-occlusion check, and they never spin
items.current: vehicles.py:260 max_blocked: float = 0.01; vehicles.py:50 prop_bodies ".*_prop" (the propellers are separate articulation bodies); quadcopter_pbr.py:563 body = f"{VEHICLE.prim}/{VEHICLE.body}" = /World/Drone/base_link, and :566/:570 take body_points and body_triangles from that prim only, so view_blocked (vehicles.py:215) never sees the *_prop link meshes or guards if they sit outside base_link (unverified: the USD asset is on NVIDIA's server). quadcopter_pbr.py:342 and :750 say the propellers are fixed joints, so the four propellers are static meshes during the whole flight: no blur disc (the Crazyflie path adds propeller blur discs, quadcopter_pbr.py:328-333, PROP_BLUR_GAIN = 1.8). The log line at quadcopter_pbr.py:587-590 reports "x% of its view on the drone itself" and will read low if props intrude.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED: no LMF2 propeller dimensions or rpm were looked up. Qualitatively, a real quadrotor shows spinning rotors as a translucent disc/streak if in view, and a camera mounted level with or behind the rotor plane sees prop tips at the frame edge. Static blades floating at a frame corner would be an obvious tell, and in the chase video (a deliverable of --cameras front back chase) a flying drone with motionless propellers looks like a parked model.
items.proposed_change: (1) From the first real probe (takeoff_front, takeoff_back at 'ground' and 'liftoff') inspect all four image corners for guard/prop pixels, and read the logged view_blocked. (2) If any intrude, build body_triangles from VEHICLE.prim (all links, transformed into the base_link frame) and feed them to mount_cameras so the mount height/stand-off search accounts for them. (3) For the chase/hero views add translucent blur discs for the LMF2 props, reusing the disc approach of drone_look.apply_drone_look, or rotate the prop xforms kinematically.
items.risk: Moving the mount changes the camera pose and the flight.camera_local quaternion consumers (camera_info.json mount block). Prop discs need the translucency path (rtx_look.py:131 enables it). The LMF2 prim hierarchy is unverified until the first Isaac run. No map rebuild.

items.title: Lens distortion, vignetting and lateral colour are typical values, not a calibrated 4 mm lens
items.current: lucid.py:99-100 "C4": Lens("4 mm f/2.8 C-mount", 4.0, 2.8, "C", k1=-0.10, k2=0.02, relative_illumination=0.55, lateral_color_px=0.8, image_circle_mm=9.0, length_mm=28.0, diameter_mm=30.0, mass_g=45.0); blur_px defaults to 0.5 (lucid.py:80); lucid.py:25-27 states the numbers are "typical of such lenses". Hand calculation: the corner is pulled in to 0.894 of its pinhole radius (-10.6 %), the corner is 55 % as bright as the centre in linear light (sRGB code value about 0.77 of the centre's), and the model has the same blur everywhere (sensor_sim.py:231), no field-dependent softening, no coma or astigmatism, no sun-induced veiling glare.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED: no datasheet or calibration for a specific 4 mm f/2.8 C-mount lens was reachable. The code's own comments say these are typical numbers; README.md:46-48 says to replace them with the owner's calibration. The sensor diagonal is hypot(2048,1536) x 3.45 um = 8.83 mm (lucid.py:232-234) against the stated 9.0 mm image circle, so there is almost no margin: a real lens at this size would show some corner falloff beyond the model.
items.proposed_change: Best fix: ask the owner for a checkerboard calibration (K, D) of the real lens and put it in lucid.LENSES; otherwise A/B with the straight-line features of the map (roads, field edges, roof ridges, cruise_front) k1 in {-0.05, -0.10, -0.20}, relative_illumination in {0.55, 0.70}, lateral_color_px in {0.4, 0.8, 1.2}. All are sensor_sim-side, so run them through camera-tool-hdr-resense without re-rendering. Add a field-dependent blur (blur_px growing to about 1.5x at the corner) as an optional experiment.
items.risk: Changing k1/k2 changes render_plan (overscan, lucid.py:206-223) and so the render size, which forces a re-render and invalidates earlier stills; keep the values fixed while testing other items. No map rebuild.

items.title: Onboard camera far clip is 10 km but the horizon terrain runs to 25 km
items.current: quadcopter_pbr.py:619 clipping_range=(0.01, 10000.0) for the front/back LUCID cameras (and :305 Gf.Vec2f(0.01, 10000.0) for the GUI view cameras, scene.py:556 for the scene cameras); the chase camera is (0.05, 20000.0) (:624) and nadir (1.0, 20000.0) (:632); world/build.py:77 --horizon default 25000.0 and build.py:385-398 horizon_ring, whose docstring says the point is that the land reaches the true horizon (about 22 km away from 40 m up). If the RTX renderer honours the camera far plane for primary rays, nothing beyond 10 km is drawn in the front and back videos, so the 10-25 km ring and the far tree lines never appear.
items.real_world: Hand calculation: horizon distance from 40 m up = sqrt(2 x 6371 km x 0.04 km) = 22.6 km (spherical Earth, no refraction; the map itself is flat). With a 10 km far plane the land would end at a depression angle of atan(40/10000) = 0.23 deg, about 5 px (at the 0.043 deg/px average) below the horizon line, leaving a band of sky between the terrain's edge and the horizon in every frame where the horizon is visible (back camera cruise: horizon about 8 deg above centre). Whether RTX clips shading at the far plane is unverified.
items.proposed_change: Set the far clip of the two onboard cameras (and the chase camera) to 40000 m (the ring is +-25 km around the route centre, so the far corner can be about 36 km from the drone), then render cruise_back and horizon views and check that the terrain meets the horizon without a sky-coloured band. If nothing changes, the far plane is not applied by RTX and this item closes as no-op. Optionally also test the near plane 0.01 m (ratio 4e6 : 1) against 0.05 m.
items.risk: Very large clip ranges can affect depth AOV precision (not used by the pipeline: only HdrColor and rgb are read). Longer rays to the 25 km ring may cost frame time. No map rebuild (camera setting only).
sources: hand calculation: d = sqrt(2 R h), R = 6371 km (standard geometry, unsourced constant)

items.title: ISP is pass-through: no colour matrix, no denoise or sharpening; noise is mild
items.current: sensor_sim.py:58 wb_gains: tuple[float, float, float] = (1.9, 1.0, 1.6); sensor_sim.py:293 raw_lin = (img / self.wb * self.masks).sum(0) then :281 demosaic(...) * self.wb, so the white balance cancels exactly and output colour equals the render's colour (module docstring :17-19 says so); no 3x3 colour matrix, no denoise, no unsharp mask, no tone curve. lucid.py:46-50: full_well_e 10500.0, read_noise_e 2.8, adc_bits 12, qe 0.64; sensor_sim.py:60 prnu 0.006. Hand calculation of the noise at the AE target (0.22 of full scale = 2264 e-): shot noise 47.6 e- = 2.1 %, about 1.25 sRGB code values (of 255) at mid-grey, about 1.5-1.7 in the red and blue channels (WB gains 1.9 / 1.6 amplify them): visible only in flat shadows, and largely removed by the crf-16 H.264 stage.
items.real_world: UNSOURCED for the Triton's colour pipeline: its ColorTransformation matrix default, Gamma default, and whether it sharpens or denoises on camera could not be read (thinklucid.com unreachable). The module docstring (lucid.py:22-23) quotes EMVA 1288 values for IMX265 cameras (10.9 ke-, 2.35 e-) without a URL; treat those as unverified. A physical Pregius colour sensor needs a colour-correction matrix and IR cut; without one hues come only from the render's albedos and sky.
items.proposed_change: Add SensorSettings fields with identity/off defaults: ccm (3x3, applied after WB, before gamma), sharpen (unsharp mask amount and sigma), denoise (small bilateral strength), black_level_dn. Probe only through camera-tool-hdr-resense: noise on/off to separate sensor noise from render noise, unsharp amount 0 / 0.3 / 0.6 with sigma 1.0 px, and a mild saturation-preserving CCM. Do NOT invent a matrix: only use one measured from a colour-checker shot of the real camera or read from its ColorTransformation registers; otherwise keep identity and record that decision.
items.risk: Sharpening and CCM change colourfulness and saturation statistics that metrics.py compares against real photos; keep them off unless a real reference justifies them. No map rebuild.

items.title: Final mp4 is near-lossless (libx264 crf 16, medium, 4:2:0) at the sensor resolution
items.current: quadcopter_pbr.py:266-270 ffmpeg -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 ... -vf scale=out_color_matrix=bt709:out_range=tv,format=yuv420p -colorspace bt709 -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -c:v libx264 -crf 16 -preset medium; frame size is the LUCID output 2048 x 1536 (lucid.py:156-160), 25 fps (:70). No bitrate cap, no GOP setting (ffmpeg default), no re-encode step, and no flag to change any of it. --save_frames keeps lossless PNGs (:88).
items.real_world: UNSOURCED: real drone video bitrates could not be fetched (dji.com unreachable, WebSearch budget exhausted). Qualitatively, footage from a real drone has been through a hardware encoder at a fixed bitrate (blocking/mosquito noise on foliage and crop rows, smeared fine noise, 4:2:0 colour), and the original LUCID output over GigE is uncompressed. Which of the two the dataset consumer expects is a decision for the owner; crf 16 favours the uncompressed look and keeps the sensor noise.
items.proposed_change: Add --video_crf (default 16) and --video_bitrate (optional, uses -b:v/-maxrate/-bufsize) to the argparse block and to VideoWriter (:252-277) and write both into camera_info.json; keep default behaviour unchanged. Offline, use ffmpeg on the saved frames or the existing mp4 to render crf 16 / 23 / 28 and an 'x Mbps' variant and compare foliage and crop-row texture on a cruise stretch. No Isaac Sim needed for the comparison if --save_frames output exists.
items.risk: Heavier compression hides the sensor noise and the DLAA artefacts the other items try to judge, so judge sharpness/noise items on PNG probe stills, not on the mp4. No map rebuild.

items.title: Motion blur and lens flare/ghosts: keep both off, verify with exposure_us (sun is out of frame)
items.current: quadcopter_pbr.py:106 --motion_blur is store_true (off); rtx_look.py:206-211 motion_blur group exposureFraction 0.5, numSamples 8, maxBlurDiameterFraction 0.02; rtx_look.py:181-197 'lens' group (bloom, vignette, grain, chromatic aberration) applies to third-person cameras only (--lens, line 105); the LUCID cameras are global shutter (lucid.py:51,92). Hand calculations: AE exposure for an average 18 % grey scene is about 256 us (sensor_sim.py:45-48,204-207 with the 100 klx assumption); worst-case image motion during that exposure is 0.21 rad/s x 256 us = 0.054 mrad = 0.06 px at the lower edge in cruise (about 0.12 px at the 500 us --exposure_us default, quadcopter_pbr.py:99). Sun elevation at 10:30 solar time, 15 July, latitude 42.0 deg is about 62 deg (declination about +21.5 deg, hour angle -22.5 deg; unsourced standard formula; the run logs the real value as 'sun N deg up'). The cameras' upper frame edge is 2.5 deg (front) and 26.5 deg (back) above the horizon in cruise, 14.5 deg at level hover, so the sun is at least 35 deg outside every frame.
items.real_world: Derived from repo constants only (no source needed for the arithmetic, but the 100 klx scene illuminance and the exposure it implies are the README's assumption, README.md:68-70, and unverified until the first run prints exposure_us). Consequence: at a few hundred microseconds a global-shutter camera shows effectively no motion blur at 10 m/s from 40 m, and with the sun 62 deg up and the optical axes pointed 8-32 deg below the horizon no sun disc, flare ghost or veiling glare belongs in these videos. Real-time RTX motion blur (a post effect from motion vectors) would add blur that the real camera would not have.
items.proposed_change: No render change. In the first probe check probe.json exposure_us < about 600 us for every cruise still; add a log warning when exposure_us > 1000 us (motion blur would then start to matter: 1 ms -> 0.2 px) and when the sun direction is within the lens field of view of any onboard camera (flare would then matter). Do not spend probe time on --motion_blur or --lens for the front/back videos.
items.risk: If the exposure assumption is wrong by 10x (exposure_us comes out above 2 ms) blur and clipping change and this item must be reopened; the README already flags exposure_us as unverified.

items.title: Tool: probe stills hold the pose (zero motion); no start offset for video; add lead-in clips
items.current: run_probe's step(t) (quadcopter_pbr.py:472-477) calls place(t) with the same t for every one of the --probe_settle frames (default 16, :112), so the drone and camera do not move between frames: history buffers see zero motion and the kept still is a best case for temporal AA, denoising and --motion_blur. A probe can take any time via flight.parse_probe (flight.py:358-364: a label '95' or 't95', must be within the flight) but --record has no start: the video loop uses t = count * sim_dt from 0 (quadcopter_pbr.py:746) and there is no --record_from/--record_to or --start. Existing: --probe (:108-111), --probe_settle (:112-113), --record (:67-68, -1 = whole flight), --fps (:70, 25 = every 8th 200 Hz step, :653). Missing: lead-in frames at video cadence, consecutive-frame output, mid-route short clips.
items.real_world: Not a real-world number. Timing facts from the repo: dt = 0.005 s (quadcopter_pbr.py:538), video cadence every = 8 physics steps (:653), so a 25-frame lead-in is 1 s of flight (10 m of travel at cruise speed) and costs 25 rendered frames per moment on top of the 17 the probe already renders.
items.proposed_change: Add --probe_lead_in SECONDS (default 0 = today's behaviour; 1.0 recommended) that, before each kept still, steps the real flight from t - lead_in to t at video cadence (every 8th step renders, ChaseCamera updated with sim_dt * every as in :766) and runs grab() on each frame, so AE and the temporal history behave as in the video; then save <camera>_<moment>.png plus <camera>_<moment>_prev1.png / _prev2.png (the two frames before) and a probe.json 'lead_in_frames' field. With a lead-in, --probe_settle can drop to 2-4. Add --record_from S and --record_to S (and --lead_in S frames discarded) to cut a segment of the video without simulating the earlier flight: set count0 = round(S / sim_dt) at :742 and t = count * sim_dt from there. Add montage.py 'frames' subcommand that tiles the 3 consecutive frames with their absolute difference.
items.risk: Per-moment time rises roughly 2x unless --probe_settle is lowered. The kinematic teleport at the first lead-in frame still produces one garbage frame (no history), so keep >= 3 lead-in frames before judging. Needs git commit of the current uncommitted probe code first (see notes). No map rebuild.

items.title: Tool: save the linear HdrColor still and re-run the sensor/ISP offline
items.current: The probe saves only the post-ISP 8-bit PNG (quadcopter_pbr.py:506-507) and probe.json (exposure_us, gain_db, saturated, mean_radiance, :510-512). The linear HdrColor tensor read by HdrReader (:388-407) is discarded after sensors[name].process(hdr) (:697). --save_raw (:102) writes the 12-bit Bayer raw but only in the --record path (:780-782), not in --probe, and a raw frame cannot be re-exposed or re-lensed. So every candidate that only touches sensor_sim.py or lucid.py (tone/AE, noise, ISP, lens model, blur, resample: items camera-tone-ae-clip, camera-lens-model-values, camera-isp-colour-noise-sharpen, part of camera-aa-resample-sharpness) needs a full Isaac Sim launch.
items.real_world: Size arithmetic from lucid.py:206-223: one HdrColor still is 2298 x 1724 x 3 float16 = 23.8 MB, so 8 moments x 2 onboard cameras is about 380 MB per probe run (npy; fp16, uncompressed). sensor_sim imports only torch and lucid (numpy), so it runs outside the Isaac app, in Isaac's Python (the tests already do, realism/run_tests.sh:30-36), CPU or GPU.
